  • Tech companies are competing fiercely for workers who can help them win the AI race.
  • We asked eight tech workers for their dream employers — and the companies they'd pass on.
  • Some favored OpenAI or Anthropic, while others preferred Big Tech.

While tech companies are pouring billions into AI infrastructure, they are also competing fiercely for AI talent — and the AI boom is reshaping the choices available to workers.

Alongside established giants like Apple, Google, and Amazon, frontier AI labs like OpenAI and Anthropic now offer the chance to work at the edge of a technological shift, with potentially significant financial upside. Meanwhile, years of tech layoffs have made job security a bigger consideration for many workers.

We asked eight tech workers about their dream employer, the Big Tech companies they're most and least interested in, and whether they've pursued jobs at OpenAI or Anthropic. (Their responses have been edited for length and clarity.)

AI labs have come calling. I haven't pursued them.Abhinav Bohra says he'd choose Amazon, with NVIDIA as his runner-up.

Abhinav Bohra

Abhinav Bohra is a senior applied scientist at Amazon. He's in his 30s and lives in Seattle.

Have you tried to land a job at an AI lab like OpenAI or Anthropic?

A couple of recruiters for AI labs have reached out to me, including one at another Big Tech company. I took the calls but never pursued them.

Labs hire people to make models smarter. I build recommendation engines, and a frontier lab has no real use for one yet: no catalog, no sellers, no shoppers to rank for. The day one of them runs an actual marketplace, people like me get very interested in them. We're not there yet.

Between Amazon, Alphabet, Microsoft, Meta, Apple, and NVIDIA, which company would you most (or least) want to work for?

Amazon, which is boring, so here's the runner-up: NVIDIA. Recommendation at scale has become an inference cost problem. Running a big model once is cheap. Running it for every search and every shopper in real time is where the money goes. When your unit of progress is the millisecond, NVIDIA sits upstream of everything.

Each company could be a good fit for someone in my field, but I also imagine they all have teams I'd love and teams I'd dread.

I'd choose Anthropic for its valuesMike Kostersitz says Anthropic would be his dream employer outside Nike.

Mike Kostersitz

Mike Kostersitz is a senior director, product management at Nike. He's in his early 60s and lives in Oregon.

If you could work for any tech company, what would it be?

If I had to look outside Nike, Anthropic would be my dream employer. The pull is real, and the company's stated values align more closely with my own than some other companies.

I took note when earlier this year, Anthropic refused a Pentagon push to strip out restrictions on mass surveillance and autonomous weapons use, a stand their own CFO said could cost the company billions in revenue. That's the kind of "values over dollars" moment most companies only talk about.

I don't expect that to hold forever. Once they IPO, the pull toward shareholder value will grow, and I'd expect other priorities to erode over time as a result. But I'd still pick Anthropic as my top choice.

Between Amazon, Alphabet, Microsoft, Meta, Apple, and NVIDIA, which company would you most (or least) want to work for?

Apple, hands down, I love the products and what the culture represents. Least would be Amazon. I have a number of friends who are current or former Amazon employees on the tech side, and not one of them has ever seemed excited to go to work there or felt like they were making a difference, beyond the paycheck being strong.

Business Insider is speaking with tech workers who've found themselves at a corporate crossroads — whether due to a layoff, resignation, job search, or shifting workplace expectations.

Share your story by filling out this form.

I haven't applied to OpenAI or AnthropicMeta's scale is part of its appeal in the competition for AI talent.

Imen Ben Youssef / Hans Lucas / AFP via Getty Images

This tech worker is a software engineer at Meta.

If you could work for any tech company, what would it be?

Honestly, the answer might be where I already am: Meta. The frontier labs get the headlines, but hyperscalers like Meta and Google are doing the same caliber of work: not just core model training and fine-tuning but building the insane infrastructure needed to serve this to billions of users.

One reason I haven't tried to land a job at an AI lab like OpenAI or Anthropic is that the labs are running on investor capital, while the hyperscalers fund their AI push from core businesses that already make enormous money. They have different risk profiles, and I've been happy with mine.

Between Amazon, Alphabet, Microsoft, Meta, Apple, and NVIDIA, which company would you most (or least) want to work for?

Most: Setting Meta aside, Google is the obvious choice for me. It's one of the few companies doing everything in-house, from TPUs to frontier models to products. That full stack under one roof is appealing.

Least: Probably Apple, and honestly that's about fit, not the company. They build incredible products and their engineering is world class, but their working model is very different from what I'm used to. Teams there tend to work on a focused slice under a lot of confidentiality, while my career so far has been end-to-end ownership, seeing a system from design through production and operations.

I'd choose SpaceX over any Big Tech company or AI labA tech lead (not pictured) in the insurance industry says SpaceX is his dream employer,

Justin Sullivan/Getty Images

This tech worker is a tech lead at a company in the insurance industry. He's in his early 40s and lives in Atlanta.

If you could work for any tech company, what would it be?

If I could work for any tech company tomorrow, I'd choose SpaceX. Few organizations on the planet operate with that level of ambition, engineering rigor, and mission clarity. Being part of a team pushing toward interplanetary travel would be an opportunity to contribute to something far bigger than any one company.

Between Amazon, Alphabet, Microsoft, Meta, Apple, and NVIDIA, which company would you most (or least) want to work for?

NVIDIA is the company I would choose. It is defining the future of accelerated computing and AI rather than reacting to it.

NVIDIA and the AI labs are compelling, but I'd still choose GoogleSachin Jain says he'd still choose Google, despite the appeal of NVIDIA and leading AI labs.

Sachin Jain

Sachin Jain is a data analyst at Google.

If you could work for any tech company, what would it be?

It would still be Google, and I'm genuinely grateful that I get to work there. That said, OpenAI and Anthropic would be incredibly compelling as well. They're at the forefront of one of the biggest technological shifts of our generation, and I think any engineer or data professional would find that exciting.

Between Amazon, Alphabet, Microsoft, Meta, Apple, and NVIDIA, which company would you most (or least) want to work for?

Aside from Google, I'd probably say NVIDIA. They've built an incredible competitive moat by creating a level of dependency across the AI ecosystem that's hard to match.

Beyond the business itself, I've always admired the culture they've cultivated. Employees don't seem to be constantly looking over their shoulders, worried about the next round of layoffs, which is becoming increasingly rare in tech. And of course, Jensen Huang is someone I really respect.

I'd rather work at a smaller employer than the hottest tech companyA software engineer (not pictured) says she'd rather have meaningful ownership at a smaller company than work for a prestigious tech giant.

aire images/Getty Images

This tech worker is a software engineer at a startup. She's in her 20s and lives in the Northeast.

If you could work for any tech company, what would it be?

What I value most today is a remote-first environment, the ability to influence what gets built, and a culture where I can spend my time solving interesting technical problems instead of navigating constant internal politics. At this stage of my career, I'd rather work at a smaller company where I have meaningful ownership than be one person in a very large organization.

Neither OpenAI nor Anthropic are particularly high on my list. I'm not especially motivated by working at whichever company is getting the most attention at the moment. Prestige and compensation alone aren't what motivate my career decisions anymore.

Between Amazon, Alphabet, Microsoft, Meta, Apple, and NVIDIA, which company would you most (or least) want to work for?

I'd probably lean toward Alphabet, Microsoft, or Apple, but the specific role would matter much more than the company name. I'm less drawn to Meta than some of the others because it has gone through significant organizational changes and layoffs in recent years.

Anthropic is my dream employer — I'd maybe pass on MicrosoftAnthropic's focus on enterprise AI is part of its appeal to some tech workers.

Illustration by Sheldon Cooper/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images

This tech worker works for a large tech company.

If you could work for any tech company, what would it be?

If I could walk into any company tomorrow, it would be Anthropic. I like that they are going after the enterprise side and actually improving specific lines of business, not just shipping a chatbot. And with the talk of them heading toward public markets, the upside is hard to ignore.

Between Amazon, Alphabet, Microsoft, Meta, Apple, and NVIDIA, which company would you most (or least) want to work for?

Most to least: Amazon, Alphabet, NVIDIA, Apple, Meta, and Microsoft last.

Microsoft is last for me because I think they are behind on AI, and it shows on the consumer product side. Copilot, from my own use and from what I hear in the market, has not landed the way it should and people are underwhelmed.

OpenAI tops my listSneja Shah says OpenAI would be her top choice outside her current employer.

Sneja Shah

Sneja Shah is a senior technical program manager at the software company Red Hat. She's in her 30s and lives in California.

If you could work for any tech company, what would it be?

If I had to look outside my current employer, OpenAI would be my top choice. The opportunity to work on products that are fundamentally changing how people work, learn, and create is incredibly exciting.

Anthropic would also be high on my list because of its emphasis on responsible AI development and long-term safety.

Between Amazon, Alphabet, Microsoft, Meta, Apple, and NVIDIA, which company would you most (or least) want to work for?

Among those companies, I'd choose NVIDIA because it's enabling nearly every major advancement in AI. Microsoft would be a close second because of how rapidly it's integrating AI across enterprise products and productivity tools.

items.title: I help people retire abroad. How to decide if it's the right move, and how to prepare.
items.summary: Federica Grazi said people are often attracted by lifestyles abroad, but don't always consider the finer details. Courtesy of Federica Grazi Retiring abroad requires more than choosing where to live. Federica Grazi, who helps retirees relocate, shared her advice for deciding whether to move and how to plan. She says trial stays and healthcare planning are vital before relocating. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Federica Grazi, 34, who is based in London. She is the founder of Mitos Relocation Solutions, an advisory firm that helps retirees move abroad. It has been edited for length and clarity. There's often a big gap between people who dream of retiring abroad and those who actually take the first step toward it. For many, hesitation gets in the way, and the idea of moving remains a dream. People are often drawn abroad by the lifestyle, but making a successful move means considering the full picture, like healthcare, aging, and the tax implications of residing in a new location. Here are the five things I recommend everyone do before they retire abroad. 1. Test-drive your potential new home Spend an extended trial period , say three months, in the place you're thinking of moving to. It's not about visiting for a week in July or August. Go in the offseason and try living like a local, thinking about what your everyday life would look like. Rent an apartment, speak with locals and expats, and join community Facebook groups. I've had clients for whom something as simple as getting medication from a pharmacy became an important test of whether they could see themselves living somewhere. 2. Turn the dream into a decision If you're unsure about retiring abroad, it doesn't have to be all or nothing. The key is not to let inertia take over and leave it as a dream, but to move from a question mark to a clear yes or no. In addition to spending a trial period in the country, you can do smaller things like speaking to others who have already moved to the destination to understand how it works in practice, or get advice from an expert who can give you a full rundown. They could even go on a scouting trip for you. Grazi said people should try to live like a local before moving to a new location. Courtesy of Federica Grazi 3. Don't rush If you decide to retire abroad and you're excited about it, don't rush the move. Changing residency is an important moment, so make a clear plan for what needs to happen before you leave. Think about whether you need a visa, housing, and even how you'll move your pet. You should also deal with things that aren't necessarily pleasant, like your will. 4. Think about taxes People often focus on the lifestyle abroad and think, "I love it here. I'll figure everything else out later." But that can lead to big tax mistakes, which need to be addressed before you move. If you only discover a problem after the tax year has ended, there might not be much you can do about it. 5. Take healthcare seriously Healthcare is something you want to be thinking about before you need it. How do you access it? How much will it cost? What might happen if you end up in the hospital? If you wait until something goes wrong, you could find yourself having to react and needing to navigate an unfamiliar healthcare system before you're fully integrated. Often, when people say they hated living abroad and moved back, it's because they didn't do enough research or preparation beforehand. Retirement abroad should be a period of joy and expansion. Doing the planning beforehand means that once you arrive, you can actually enjoy it. Read the original article on Business Insider

Courtesy of Federica Grazi

  • Retiring abroad requires more than choosing where to live.
  • Federica Grazi, who helps retirees relocate, shared her advice for deciding whether to move and how to plan.
  • She says trial stays and healthcare planning are vital before relocating.

This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Federica Grazi, 34, who is based in London. She is the founder of Mitos Relocation Solutions, an advisory firm that helps retirees move abroad. It has been edited for length and clarity.

There's often a big gap between people who dream of retiring abroad and those who actually take the first step toward it. For many, hesitation gets in the way, and the idea of moving remains a dream.

People are often drawn abroad by the lifestyle, but making a successful move means considering the full picture, like healthcare, aging, and the tax implications of residing in a new location.

Here are the five things I recommend everyone do before they retire abroad.

1. Test-drive your potential new home

Spend an extended trial period, say three months, in the place you're thinking of moving to. It's not about visiting for a week in July or August. Go in the offseason and try living like a local, thinking about what your everyday life would look like.

Rent an apartment, speak with locals and expats, and join community Facebook groups.

I've had clients for whom something as simple as getting medication from a pharmacy became an important test of whether they could see themselves living somewhere.

2. Turn the dream into a decision

If you're unsure about retiring abroad, it doesn't have to be all or nothing. The key is not to let inertia take over and leave it as a dream, but to move from a question mark to a clear yes or no.

In addition to spending a trial period in the country, you can do smaller things like speaking to others who have already moved to the destination to understand how it works in practice, or get advice from an expert who can give you a full rundown. They could even go on a scouting trip for you.

Grazi said people should try to live like a local before moving to a new location.

Courtesy of Federica Grazi

3. Don't rush

If you decide to retire abroad and you're excited about it, don't rush the move. Changing residency is an important moment, so make a clear plan for what needs to happen before you leave.

Think about whether you need a visa, housing, and even how you'll move your pet. You should also deal with things that aren't necessarily pleasant, like your will.

4. Think about taxes

People often focus on the lifestyle abroad and think, "I love it here. I'll figure everything else out later." But that can lead to big tax mistakes, which need to be addressed before you move.

If you only discover a problem after the tax year has ended, there might not be much you can do about it.

5. Take healthcare seriously

Healthcare is something you want to be thinking about before you need it. How do you access it? How much will it cost? What might happen if you end up in the hospital?

If you wait until something goes wrong, you could find yourself having to react and needing to navigate an unfamiliar healthcare system before you're fully integrated.

Often, when people say they hated living abroad and moved back, it's because they didn't do enough research or preparation beforehand.

Retirement abroad should be a period of joy and expansion. Doing the planning beforehand means that once you arrive, you can actually enjoy it.

items.title: A financially independent couple shares 3 money rules that helped them pay off debt and build wealth
items.summary: Brittany and Kelan Kline are the cofounders of The Savvy Couple. Kelan Kline Kelan and Brittany Kline built The Savvy Couple blog into a seven-figure online business success. They achieved a $1 million net worth by balancing income growth with controlled lifestyle spending. "We make a plan for our money every month," Kelan said. For Kelan and Brittany Kline, improving their finances came down to a simple idea: widen the gap between what they earned and what they spent. The couple, who once worked traditional jobs as a jail deputy and elementary school teacher, were newly married and carrying roughly $40,000 in student-loan debt when they began rethinking their finances . They attacked both sides of the equation. On the income side, they built The Savvy Couple , a personal-finance blog that eventually grew into a seven-figure online business . On the spending side, they focused on keeping their lifestyle relatively stable as their income increased. The couple said their household net worth — including the estimated value of their businesses, investments, and primary residence — surpassed $1 million in 2020. Business Insider reviewed a screenshot from their Rocket Money account showing a seven-figure net worth. Here are three principles they said helped them spend less without feeling permanently deprived. 1. Think about what a purchase costs in time One of the biggest shifts for the Klines was mental. They started thinking about purchases not simply in dollars, but in hours of work. "We had a realization that, with our 9-to-5s, we were trading our time for money," Kelan told Business Insider. "Every purchase we had, we were not actually paying for it with money. We were actually paying it with our time." A $50,000 truck, for example, might represent months of work. A $100 dinner might translate into several hours on the job. "It kind of gives you that perspective of, 'Is this worth my time to purchase it?'" he said. 2. Know the difference between frugal and cheap The Klines don't equate frugality with always buying the least expensive option. "There's a very distinct difference between being cheap and frugal," Kelan said. A cheap shopper, for example, might buy the least expensive vacuum and have to replace it repeatedly. A frugal shopper, on the other hand, might pay more upfront for something that offers better value and lasts longer. The goal, he said, is to ask which option provides the most value without costing unnecessarily more. The Klines reside in Rochester, New York, where they met in high school. Courtesy of The Klines That mindset also helped them resist lifestyle inflation as their earnings grew. They stayed in their starter home for seven years, drove used cars, rarely ate out, and spent roughly five years as a one-car household. "You don't have to increase your lifestyle to be happy," Kelan said. Rather than succumb to lifestyle inflation, they directed more of the growing gap between their income and expenses toward debt repayment and investments. 3. Give every dollar a job — including fun money The Klines still track their spending and stick to a monthly budget. "We make a plan for our money every month," Kelan said. While some people view budgeting as restrictive, they see it differently: "When you give yourself a budget and make a plan every month, you're actually giving yourself freedom to spend the money where you want it and where you get the most joy and fulfillment from." That includes discretionary spending. For example, Brittany enjoys buying coffee, so the couple deliberately builds personal spending money into their budget. Today, they said, each of them gets about $200 a month to spend however they want, up from roughly $100 earlier in their journey. The point isn't to eliminate everything enjoyable, but to cut more aggressively in areas that matter less while preserving spending they value. Sometimes the sacrifice is temporary The couple did go through periods of much stricter spending, particularly when they were focused on eliminating their student loans. "Sometimes it's temporary pain to get to the end goal that you want," Kelan said. He remembers declining invitations to eat out or meet friends for drinks and cutting restaurant spending to roughly once a month. "We sacrificed a ton when we were paying off debt." The key, in his view, was knowing that the restrictions had an endpoint. Rather than thinking they would live that way forever, they treated the cuts as a short-term sprint toward a specific goal. Once the debt was gone, money that had previously gone toward loan payments could instead be invested or spent on things they valued more. Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: Warren Buffett is 96. Take a look at the business legend's remarkable life.
items.summary: Warren Buffett is the chairman and former CEO of Berkshire Hathaway. Daniel Zuchnik / Getty Images It's Warren Buffett's 96th birthday, his first since stepping down as Berkshire Hathaway CEO. The legendary investor bought his first stock at 11 and built a $1 trillion company. Buffett made billions by investing in stocks like Coca-Cola and buying businesses like Geico. It's Warren Buffett's 96th birthday, his first since stepping down as Berkshire Hathaway CEO. He remains chairman of the storied company. Buffett retired from the top job at the turn of this year, marking the end of an era that saw the legendary investor transform a failing textile mill into a $1 trillion conglomerate over six decades. Here's a look back at Buffett's remarkable life. Born to do business A family heads to California during the Great Depression. Bettmann/Getty Images Buffett was born in Omaha, Nebraska, on August 30, 1930, at the height of the Great Depression. He was the second of three children and the only son of Howard, a stockbroker and later a congressman, and Leila, a homemaker. The investor started his business career at six, selling Juicy Fruit chewing gum door to door. He later resold individual bottles of Coca-Cola from a pack, delivered newspapers, and built up a pinball machine business, which he later sold. Buffett was 11 when he bought his first stock, Cities Service Preferred, and filed his first tax return at 13. He bought a farm at 14 and rented it to a tenant farmer. When he was 16, he had amassed $5,000, around $85,000 in today's money. Learning from the best Woodrow Wilson High School; Bill Pugliano/Getty Buffett majored in business at Wharton before transferring to the University of Nebraska-Lincoln and graduating in 1950, at the age of 19. Around that time, he read Benjamin Graham's "The Intelligent Investor," which introduced him to the key tenets of value investing, such as buying stocks so cheap that they provide a "margin of safety." Buffett enrolled at Columbia Business School after learning Graham taught there. After graduating, he worked for his father's company for a year before joining Graham's investment firm, where he received a masterclass in analyzing companies and identifying bargain stocks. In 1952, at age 22, he married a college student, Susan Thompson, and the pair had their first child, Susan or "Little Susie," in 1953. He began teaching night classes on investing and inviting family and friends to invest their money with him. In 1956, as Graham prepared to retire, Buffett moved back to Omaha and prepared to launch his firm, Buffett Partnership. Buying and building KMTV Omaha/Jeremy Harris Lipschultz/YouTube Buffett embraced Graham's trademark "cigar butt" approach of sniffing out cheap stocks with "one last puff" of value, such as Sanborn Map Company and Dempster Mill Manufacturing. His partnership's assets grew from about $100,000 to $20 million as his outperformance attracted more investors and his returns compounded. He and his wife had their second child, Howard, in 1954, and their third, Peter, in 1958. Buffett also met Charlie Munger in 1959, who encouraged him to shift from buying dirt-cheap businesses to "wonderful companies at fair prices." In 1962, Buffett began acquiring shares of Berkshire Hathaway, a struggling textile mill. He seized control of the company in 1965 after its management agreed to buy him out, then tried to shortchange him. Buffett Partnership also invested in American Express after its stock plunged during the Salad Oil Scandal, and in Disney after Walt Disney gave Buffett a personal tour of Disneyland and sold the investor on his vision. Partnerships, old and new A billboard welcoming Berkshire Hathaway shareholders displays a vintage picture of Chairman Buffett and Vice Chairman Munger at the company's annual meeting in Omaha Thomson Reuters Buffett acquired insurers such as National Indemnity, paving the way for him to use "float" — premiums collected before claims are paid — as a source of low-cost, permanent capital for investing. In 1969, the investor grew concerned about overvalued assets and a lack of compelling opportunities, so he decided to wind down his Buffett Partnership and return his partners' money while retaining a significant stake in Berkshire. The firm's assets had reached $104 million in 1970, reflecting, in part, a compounded annual return of 31% since 1956. Buffett invested in the Illinois Bank and Trust Company in 1969, acquired See's Candies in 1972, built a stake in the Washington Post Company, and bet on other businesses such as Blue Chip Stamps. Munger also became his formal business partner and joined Berkshire as vice-chair. By age 45, Buffett's wealth had grown to about $34 million, or roughly $210 million today. Deals of a lifetime NBC News Berkshire invested in car insurer Geico and other companies such as Capital Cities/ABC and Wesco Financial, as Buffett began seeking out businesses with "moats" or durable competitive advantages. His wife moved to San Francisco in 1977 to pursue singing and activism. She introduced Buffett to a friend, Astrid Menks, who moved in with Buffett and took care of him, and whom Buffett would marry after Susan died in 2004. In 1983, Berkshire acquired Nebraska Furniture Mart . In 1985, Buffett became a billionaire at age 55, appearing on the Forbes 400 list that year. Status and scandals Warren Buffett, 1995 AP Images Buffett's yearly shareholder letters, colorful interviews, and annual shareholder gatherings made him a celebrity and earned him the moniker the "Oracle of Omaha." He had built a billion-dollar stake in Coca-Cola by 1989, drawn by its global brand, pricing power, and cash generation. He also invested in Gillette and established a stake in Wells Fargo. Buffett met Bill Gates at a 4th of July event in 1991 and became fast friends with the Microsoft cofounder. He also stepped in as interim chairman of Salomon Brothers after a Treasury bond scandal threatened his investment in the bank. He delivered a message to employees in testimony to Congress in 1991: "Lose money for the firm, and I will be understanding. Lose a shred of reputation for the firm, and I will be ruthless." Buffett's buying spree Warren Buffett, chairman of Berkshire Hathaway, sits in the front row with his wife Susan before the opening of the annual Berkshire Hathaway shareholders meeting in Omaha, Neb., Saturday, April 28, 2001. AP/Nati Harnik Berkshire acquired the other half of Geico for $2.3 billion in 1996, paid $22 billion in stock to take over reinsurer General Re in 1998, and led an investor group to buy MidAmerican Energy in 1999. Buffett capitalized on the dot-com crash, scooping up Benjamin Moore in 2000, Shaw Carpets in 2001, Fruit of the Loom and Pampered Chef in 2002, and Clayton Homes in 2003. Capitalizing on crisis Berkshire Hathaway CEO Warren Buffett (L) gestures before a table tennis game with Microsoft Chairman Bill Gates in Omaha May 5, 2013 the day after the company's annual meeting. Rick Wilking/Reuters After Susan's death in 2004, Buffett made philanthropy a greater priority. In 2006, he pledged the vast majority of his Berkshire stock to the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation and four of his family's foundations, foreshadowing his cofounding of the Giving Pledge in 2010. Buffett continued to make acquisitions, including Iscar, an Israeli precision toolmaker, in 2006, and Marmon, an industrial conglomerate, in 2007. He also acquired BNSF Railway for $34 billion in 2010: Berkshire's largest acquisition up to that point. During the financial crisis, Berkshire's cash reserves, risk management, and willingness to "be greedy when others are fearful" led to a flurry of lucrative deals with Goldman Sachs, General Electric, Dow Chemical, Mars, Harley-Davidson, and other companies. Buffett hired Todd Combs in 2010 and Ted Weschler in 2011 as investment managers to help him oversee Berkshire's stock portfolio. A year later, he was diagnosed with prostate cancer and underwent successful radiation treatment. He also gained public prominence for supporting a "Buffett Rule" that would close loopholes to prevent situations like his own, where his secretary paid a higher tax rate than he did. Berkshire partnered with 3G Capital to acquire Heinz, which later became Kraft Heinz, for $23 billion in 2013. Preparing for a new era Warren Buffett at the Berkshire Hathaway annual shareholders' meeting in Omaha, Nebraska, on May 3, 2024. Scott Morgan/REUTERS In 2015, Berkshire made its biggest deal yet when it shelled out $37 billion for Precision Castparts. Between 2016 and 2018, Berkshire spent around $36 billion to build a roughly 5% stake in Apple, which more than quadrupled in value to above $170 billion by 2023, making it easily Berkshire's number-one holding and one of the most lucrative bets in its history. Berkshire has pared the position by about 75% over the past three years . The COVID-19 pandemic prompted Buffett to cash out his stakes in the "Big Four" US airlines. But he's made several big bets since, such as buying Dominion Energy's natural gas assets for $10 billion, purchasing stakes in five of the largest Japanese trading companies, and acquiring Alleghany for $12 billion, which added businesses such as Squishmallows-maker Jazwares to Berkshire's stable. Berkshire also paid more than $11 billion over about seven years to acquire Pilot Flying J, a truck-stop chain that had been one of the country's biggest private companies. Buffett lost his right-hand man and one of his closest friends when Munger died in November 2023, a few weeks shy of his 100th birthday and still in the job. Berkshire's market cap breached $1 trillion in late 2024, ranking it among the world's most valuable companies. During Buffett's tenure as CEO, Berkshire's shares rose by 6,100,000% or nearly 20% a year between 1964 and 2025, far above the benchmark S&P 500's roughly 46,000% or 10.5% annual return with dividends included over the same period. Buffett prepared his shareholders for his departure, outlining his estate plan and naming Greg Abel, Berkshire's head of non-insurance operations, as his successor in 2021. But he still stunned the business world in May 2025 when he announced that he would step down as CEO at the end of the year. 10. New era begins Two Warren Buffett fans outside of his home. Theron Mohamed/Business Insider Abel succeeded Buffett as Berkshire's CEO on New Year's Day 2026, marking the end of Buffett's 55-year tenure. But Buffett remains the company's chair, and still comes to the office five days a week. He wasn't on stage at Berkshire's shareholder meeting this year, but spoke briefly to thank outgoing Apple CEO Tim Cook and sat for a live interview on the day. It was clear to this reporter after spending a few days in Buffett's hometown of Omaha that his legacy would live on . Buffett made the call to invest in Google's parent company, Alphabet, in the third quarter of last year. Berkshire has grown that stake to nearly $38 billion as of June 30, making Alphabet the third-biggest position in its stock portfolio after Apple and American Express. The business icon, who has given away more than half of his wealth since 2006, has charged his children with giving away virtually all of his remaining $144 billion fortune to worthy causes by the end of 2034. items.summary_html:
Warren Buffett is the chairman and former CEO of Berkshire Hathaway.

Daniel Zuchnik / Getty Images

  • It's Warren Buffett's 96th birthday, his first since stepping down as Berkshire Hathaway CEO.
  • The legendary investor bought his first stock at 11 and built a $1 trillion company.
  • Buffett made billions by investing in stocks like Coca-Cola and buying businesses like Geico.

It's Warren Buffett's 96th birthday, his first since stepping down as Berkshire Hathaway CEO. He remains chairman of the storied company.

Buffett retired from the top job at the turn of this year, marking the end of an era that saw the legendary investor transform a failing textile mill into a $1 trillion conglomerate over six decades.

Here's a look back at Buffett's remarkable life.

Born to do business
A family heads to California during the Great Depression.

Bettmann/Getty Images

Buffett was born in Omaha, Nebraska, on August 30, 1930, at the height of the Great Depression. He was the second of three children and the only son of Howard, a stockbroker and later a congressman, and Leila, a homemaker.

The investor started his business career at six, selling Juicy Fruit chewing gum door to door. He later resold individual bottles of Coca-Cola from a pack, delivered newspapers, and built up a pinball machine business, which he later sold.

Buffett was 11 when he bought his first stock, Cities Service Preferred, and filed his first tax return at 13. He bought a farm at 14 and rented it to a tenant farmer.

When he was 16, he had amassed $5,000, around $85,000 in today's money.

Learning from the best

Woodrow Wilson High School; Bill Pugliano/Getty

Buffett majored in business at Wharton before transferring to the University of Nebraska-Lincoln and graduating in 1950, at the age of 19.

Around that time, he read Benjamin Graham's "The Intelligent Investor," which introduced him to the key tenets of value investing, such as buying stocks so cheap that they provide a "margin of safety."

Buffett enrolled at Columbia Business School after learning Graham taught there. After graduating, he worked for his father's company for a year before joining Graham's investment firm, where he received a masterclass in analyzing companies and identifying bargain stocks.

In 1952, at age 22, he married a college student, Susan Thompson, and the pair had their first child, Susan or "Little Susie," in 1953. He began teaching night classes on investing and inviting family and friends to invest their money with him. In 1956, as Graham prepared to retire, Buffett moved back to Omaha and prepared to launch his firm, Buffett Partnership.

Buying and building

KMTV Omaha/Jeremy Harris Lipschultz/YouTube

Buffett embraced Graham's trademark "cigar butt" approach of sniffing out cheap stocks with "one last puff" of value, such as Sanborn Map Company and Dempster Mill Manufacturing. His partnership's assets grew from about $100,000 to $20 million as his outperformance attracted more investors and his returns compounded.

He and his wife had their second child, Howard, in 1954, and their third, Peter, in 1958. Buffett also met Charlie Munger in 1959, who encouraged him to shift from buying dirt-cheap businesses to "wonderful companies at fair prices."

In 1962, Buffett began acquiring shares of Berkshire Hathaway, a struggling textile mill. He seized control of the company in 1965 after its management agreed to buy him out, then tried to shortchange him.

Buffett Partnership also invested in American Express after its stock plunged during the Salad Oil Scandal, and in Disney after Walt Disney gave Buffett a personal tour of Disneyland and sold the investor on his vision.

Partnerships, old and new
A billboard welcoming Berkshire Hathaway shareholders displays a vintage picture of Chairman Buffett and Vice Chairman Munger at the company's annual meeting in Omaha

Thomson Reuters

Buffett acquired insurers such as National Indemnity, paving the way for him to use "float" — premiums collected before claims are paid — as a source of low-cost, permanent capital for investing.

In 1969, the investor grew concerned about overvalued assets and a lack of compelling opportunities, so he decided to wind down his Buffett Partnership and return his partners' money while retaining a significant stake in Berkshire. The firm's assets had reached $104 million in 1970, reflecting, in part, a compounded annual return of 31% since 1956.

Buffett invested in the Illinois Bank and Trust Company in 1969, acquired See's Candies in 1972, built a stake in the Washington Post Company, and bet on other businesses such as Blue Chip Stamps. Munger also became his formal business partner and joined Berkshire as vice-chair.

By age 45, Buffett's wealth had grown to about $34 million, or roughly $210 million today.

Deals of a lifetime

NBC News

Berkshire invested in car insurer Geico and other companies such as Capital Cities/ABC and Wesco Financial, as Buffett began seeking out businesses with "moats" or durable competitive advantages.

His wife moved to San Francisco in 1977 to pursue singing and activism. She introduced Buffett to a friend, Astrid Menks, who moved in with Buffett and took care of him, and whom Buffett would marry after Susan died in 2004.

In 1983, Berkshire acquired Nebraska Furniture Mart. In 1985, Buffett became a billionaire at age 55, appearing on the Forbes 400 list that year.

Status and scandals
Warren Buffett, 1995

AP Images

Buffett's yearly shareholder letters, colorful interviews, and annual shareholder gatherings made him a celebrity and earned him the moniker the "Oracle of Omaha."

He had built a billion-dollar stake in Coca-Cola by 1989, drawn by its global brand, pricing power, and cash generation. He also invested in Gillette and established a stake in Wells Fargo.

Buffett met Bill Gates at a 4th of July event in 1991 and became fast friends with the Microsoft cofounder. He also stepped in as interim chairman of Salomon Brothers after a Treasury bond scandal threatened his investment in the bank. He delivered a message to employees in testimony to Congress in 1991: "Lose money for the firm, and I will be understanding. Lose a shred of reputation for the firm, and I will be ruthless."

Buffett's buying spree
Warren Buffett, chairman of Berkshire Hathaway, sits in the front row with his wife Susan before the opening of the annual Berkshire Hathaway shareholders meeting in Omaha, Neb., Saturday, April 28, 2001.

AP/Nati Harnik

Berkshire acquired the other half of Geico for $2.3 billion in 1996, paid $22 billion in stock to take over reinsurer General Re in 1998, and led an investor group to buy MidAmerican Energy in 1999.

Buffett capitalized on the dot-com crash, scooping up Benjamin Moore in 2000, Shaw Carpets in 2001, Fruit of the Loom and Pampered Chef in 2002, and Clayton Homes in 2003.

Capitalizing on crisis
Berkshire Hathaway CEO Warren Buffett (L) gestures before a table tennis game with Microsoft Chairman Bill Gates in Omaha May 5, 2013 the day after the company's annual meeting.

Rick Wilking/Reuters

After Susan's death in 2004, Buffett made philanthropy a greater priority. In 2006, he pledged the vast majority of his Berkshire stock to the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation and four of his family's foundations, foreshadowing his cofounding of the Giving Pledge in 2010.

Buffett continued to make acquisitions, including Iscar, an Israeli precision toolmaker, in 2006, and Marmon, an industrial conglomerate, in 2007. He also acquired BNSF Railway for $34 billion in 2010: Berkshire's largest acquisition up to that point.

During the financial crisis, Berkshire's cash reserves, risk management, and willingness to "be greedy when others are fearful" led to a flurry of lucrative deals with Goldman Sachs, General Electric, Dow Chemical, Mars, Harley-Davidson, and other companies.

Buffett hired Todd Combs in 2010 and Ted Weschler in 2011 as investment managers to help him oversee Berkshire's stock portfolio. A year later, he was diagnosed with prostate cancer and underwent successful radiation treatment. He also gained public prominence for supporting a "Buffett Rule" that would close loopholes to prevent situations like his own, where his secretary paid a higher tax rate than he did.

Berkshire partnered with 3G Capital to acquire Heinz, which later became Kraft Heinz, for $23 billion in 2013.

Preparing for a new era
Warren Buffett at the Berkshire Hathaway annual shareholders' meeting in Omaha, Nebraska, on May 3, 2024.

Scott Morgan/REUTERS

In 2015, Berkshire made its biggest deal yet when it shelled out $37 billion for Precision Castparts. Between 2016 and 2018, Berkshire spent around $36 billion to build a roughly 5% stake in Apple, which more than quadrupled in value to above $170 billion by 2023, making it easily Berkshire's number-one holding and one of the most lucrative bets in its history. Berkshire has pared the position by about 75% over the past three years.

The COVID-19 pandemic prompted Buffett to cash out his stakes in the "Big Four" US airlines. But he's made several big bets since, such as buying Dominion Energy's natural gas assets for $10 billion, purchasing stakes in five of the largest Japanese trading companies, and acquiring Alleghany for $12 billion, which added businesses such as Squishmallows-maker Jazwares to Berkshire's stable.

Berkshire also paid more than $11 billion over about seven years to acquire Pilot Flying J, a truck-stop chain that had been one of the country's biggest private companies.

Buffett lost his right-hand man and one of his closest friends when Munger died in November 2023, a few weeks shy of his 100th birthday and still in the job.

Berkshire's market cap breached $1 trillion in late 2024, ranking it among the world's most valuable companies.

During Buffett's tenure as CEO, Berkshire's shares rose by 6,100,000% or nearly 20% a year between 1964 and 2025, far above the benchmark S&P 500's roughly 46,000% or 10.5% annual return with dividends included over the same period.

Buffett prepared his shareholders for his departure, outlining his estate plan and naming Greg Abel, Berkshire's head of non-insurance operations, as his successor in 2021.

But he still stunned the business world in May 2025 when he announced that he would step down as CEO at the end of the year.

10. New era begins
Two Warren Buffett fans outside of his home.

Theron Mohamed/Business Insider

Abel succeeded Buffett as Berkshire's CEO on New Year's Day 2026, marking the end of Buffett's 55-year tenure. But Buffett remains the company's chair, and still comes to the office five days a week.

He wasn't on stage at Berkshire's shareholder meeting this year, but spoke briefly to thank outgoing Apple CEO Tim Cook and sat for a live interview on the day. It was clear to this reporter after spending a few days in Buffett's hometown of Omaha that his legacy would live on.

Buffett made the call to invest in Google's parent company, Alphabet, in the third quarter of last year. Berkshire has grown that stake to nearly $38 billion as of June 30, making Alphabet the third-biggest position in its stock portfolio after Apple and American Express.

The business icon, who has given away more than half of his wealth since 2006, has charged his children with giving away virtually all of his remaining $144 billion fortune to worthy causes by the end of 2034.

items.title: Our kids are college graduates, but we're paying their rent. We understand what they're up against.
items.summary: The author (second from left) said she and her husband are paying rent for their 20-something kids to help give them a strong foundation for their futures. Courtesy of Cherith Glover Fluker. My children are college graduates. I'm still paying their rent, and I'm OK with that. A college degree may be an important step toward financial stability, but it takes time to accumulate and transfer wealth. We cover rent, but the help comes with conversations, actionable planning, and an end date. When our youngest child graduated from college, my husband and I were overwhelmed with pride. There we were, two first-generation college graduates who had somehow managed to get both of our children through college. But right next to that pride was another emotion: fear. We weren't afraid that they wouldn't be successful; we've always believed in them. Our fear stemmed from knowing that a college degree doesn't always translate into financial stability. That's especially true for some Black graduates entering a financial system that hasn't historically given Black families the same opportunities to build and pass down wealth. So, while I proudly watched my kids cross the stage to receive their diplomas, I was already thinking about what would come next. For us, that means continuing to pay their rent while they get their footing. We've put thought into this decision Our decision to pay our grown children's rent — ages 23 and 25 — may look like coddling to some people. But for us, it's intentional. Neither mine nor my husband's parents went to college, and we didn't have very many people to call when things got tight. Over the years, we've built a comfortable life without a safety net, one paycheck at a time. We're using that comfort to give our children the runway we never had. Do you have a hot take on a common parenting belief? Email Jennifer Beck Goldblatt at jgoldblatt@insider.com to share your experience with Business Insider. There's data that backs up what my husband and I already know from experience. According to the National Center for Education Statistics, Black college graduates , age 25 to 34, earn roughly $14,000 less per year than their white peers with the same degree. Additionally, more of them graduate with debt, with 52% of Black students graduating with at least $25,000 in student loan debt compared to 41% of white students according to a Survey of Consumer Finances by the Federal Reserve. Even with our help, our children graduated with a small amount of student loan debt. Our support comes with a plan To give them both time to focus on building their careers and saving money, we pay their rent. Of course, this arrangement comes with a caveat. We talk openly about finances and set concrete goals to help them get closer to financial independence . Our conversations include a phase-out timeline, with a goal of ending our rent support six months to a year after they have consistently worked and saved, so they understand that their rent coverage isn't indefinite. This is something we'll reevaluate as a family over time. The author said she wants to take the pressure off of her children as they build their careers and find their footing. Courtesy of Cherith Glover Fluker. We've set emergency fund targets and worked through credit-building strategies together. We even encourage them to save a little more anytime they can, so they're building a cushion of their own. To keep them motivated along the way and moving toward the finish line, we celebrate every milestone, such as reaching a savings goal or paying off a debt. We're buying them time We're not the only family doing this. A survey by AARP found that 75% of parents with a child age 18 or older support them in some way. A February 2026 Pew Research Center study found that nearly half of Black adults ages 18-29 (47%) reported they received financial assistance from family in the previous year. Our plan isn't perfect, but we stand by it. Our intention is not to try and shield our children from the real world. We simply want to buy them time. Instead of worrying about a missed rent payment, they can focus on building their careers. We want to give them a foundation sturdy enough that, one day, they can build that bridge — or a stronger one — for their own kids. Read the original article on Business Insider

But right next to that pride was another emotion: fear.

We weren't afraid that they wouldn't be successful; we've always believed in them. Our fear stemmed from knowing that a college degree doesn't always translate into financial stability. That's especially true for some Black graduates entering a financial system that hasn't historically given Black families the same opportunities to build and pass down wealth.

So, while I proudly watched my kids cross the stage to receive their diplomas, I was already thinking about what would come next. For us, that means continuing to pay their rent while they get their footing.

We've put thought into this decision

Our decision to pay our grown children's rent — ages 23 and 25 — may look like coddling to some people. But for us, it's intentional. Neither mine nor my husband's parents went to college, and we didn't have very many people to call when things got tight. Over the years, we've built a comfortable life without a safety net, one paycheck at a time. We're using that comfort to give our children the runway we never had.

Do you have a hot take on a common parenting belief? Email Jennifer Beck Goldblatt at jgoldblatt@insider.com to share your experience with Business Insider.

There's data that backs up what my husband and I already know from experience. According to the National Center for Education Statistics, Black college graduates, age 25 to 34, earn roughly $14,000 less per year than their white peers with the same degree. Additionally, more of them graduate with debt, with 52% of Black students graduating with at least $25,000 in student loan debt compared to 41% of white students according to a Survey of Consumer Finances by the Federal Reserve.

Even with our help, our children graduated with a small amount of student loan debt.

Our support comes with a plan

To give them both time to focus on building their careers and saving money, we pay their rent. Of course, this arrangement comes with a caveat. We talk openly about finances and set concrete goals to help them get closer to financial independence. Our conversations include a phase-out timeline, with a goal of ending our rent support six months to a year after they have consistently worked and saved, so they understand that their rent coverage isn't indefinite. This is something we'll reevaluate as a family over time.

The author said she wants to take the pressure off of her children as they build their careers and find their footing.

Courtesy of Cherith Glover Fluker.

We've set emergency fund targets and worked through credit-building strategies together. We even encourage them to save a little more anytime they can, so they're building a cushion of their own. To keep them motivated along the way and moving toward the finish line, we celebrate every milestone, such as reaching a savings goal or paying off a debt.

We're buying them time

We're not the only family doing this. A survey by AARP found that 75% of parents with a child age 18 or older support them in some way. A February 2026 Pew Research Center study found that nearly half of Black adults ages 18-29 (47%) reported they received financial assistance from family in the previous year.

Our plan isn't perfect, but we stand by it. Our intention is not to try and shield our children from the real world. We simply want to buy them time. Instead of worrying about a missed rent payment, they can focus on building their careers. We want to give them a foundation sturdy enough that, one day, they can build that bridge — or a stronger one — for their own kids.

items.title: 12 jobs that are set to shrink over the next decade
items.summary: Employment of telemarkers is projected to fall from 2025 to 2035. Maskot/Getty Images The Bureau of Labor Statistics published new job projections for 2025 to 2035. Employment of word processors and typists is expected to fall the quickest. Automation is a key reason some of the jobs are expected to decline. Automation is set to reduce the need for some jobs over the next decade, like order clerks and switchboard operators. New Bureau of Labor Statistics projections show which jobs may rapidly grow between 2025 and 2035, and which may shrink. Word processors and typists are projected to experience the largest percent decline, falling 34%. It's one of 206 jobs that the Bureau of Labor Statistics classified as having "very high" exposure to AI . The 12 jobs with the largest projected percent declines typically aren't high-paying. Most of them earned less than the national median annual wage of $50,980 in 2025. Employment of foundry mold and coremakers, as well as metal and plastic patternmakers, is projected to decline, partly due to businesses' ability to leverage 3D printers . For word processors and typists, BLS said other workers are taking on these duties, and "traditional typing methods continue to be replaced by automated processes through use of machine learning (ML) technologies." Telemarketers and mining roof bolters are set to see changes in demand for different reasons. For telemarketers, BLS said the "share decreases as the Do Not Call registry from the FCC continues to grow, and companies increasingly use alternative digital marketing methods." For roof bolters, it's due to a preference for surface mining over underground work. Overall, US employment is projected to rise 3.5% over the decade, down from 10.9% growth in the decade earlier. Some jobs are expected to increase due to the care of an aging population . The private healthcare and social assistance sector is expected to have a bounty of opportunities, accounting for 37% of the 5.9 million jobs projected to be added to the US. items.title: British soldiers are figuring out where flying drones and ground robots fall short
items.summary: The US Army and its partners and allies recently tested drones and other emerging technologies at an exercise at Fort Irwin, California. US Army photo by Sgt. Nathan Arellano Tlaczani British soldiers say that different types of drones present different types of challenges. Ground drones can be too costly, and aerial drones can have issues with power, loitering time, and range. I was on the ground at a recent testing ground where troops put models through their paces — and told me about pros and cons. British soldiers are testing the trade-offs of using drones both in the air and on the ground — and the challenges that come with each. At a recent US-led exercise in the Mojave Desert , thousands of soldiers gathered to try out new technologies, including uncrewed systems. British troops at the training were experimenting with which types of drones were best suited to specific tactics and missions, and shared what they most want from these systems. Lessons from the exercise included how systems performed in extreme heat and on rugged desert terrain, whether soldiers had enough drones for their missions amid electronic warfare and connectivity issues, and how drones can be most useful. The British Army's current experimentation unit, the 2nd Battalion, The Yorkshire Regiment, was present at the exercise alongside the unit that will take over their experimentation role, the 1st Battalion Irish Guards. The latter unit also has experience with drones, including a recent exercise with Ukrainian forces. Business Insider also attended the exercises. Capt. Wick Willett, a mortar platoon commander with the 1st Battalion Irish Guards, said he and his troops had seen the strengths and weaknesses of drones. "I think there are challenges with both air and ground vehicles," Willett told Business Insider, adding that what helps work through those issues are "these robust trials that we're going through now." The British Army approaches testing of drone systems through two different processes: experimentation and trials. Trials are designed to take a drone, "put it through its paces, and test it to see if it does what the Army wants it to do" before it's acquired, Lt. Col. John Black, commander of the 2nd Battalion of the Yorkshire Regiment, told Business Insider. This includes safety and integration tests. Experiments are more focused on applying a system to specific use cases, such as ground robots to make front-line logistics easier or safer, or aerial drones for reconnaissance. In drone experiments, British soldiers see how systems work in specific situations. US Army photo by Sgt. Nathan Arellano Tlaczani Willett said he noticed the need for uncrewed ground vehicles to be more consumable, meaning troops could be able to use, lose, or break them more flexibly without worrying about the costs or feasibility of replacing them, "and in order to be consumable, they need to be at a certain price point per unit." Other soldiers expressed similar sentiments about ground robots, saying the systems could sometimes feel too high-end to use effectively in tactical settings. Black said his experience after testing dozens of UGVs was that the systems were often too expensive to be used in larger volumes and be expended. Other issues with ground vehicles include driving over certain terrain, the impact of heat on systems and batteries, and the types of missions that are best suited, such as logistics runs and breaches that could be too dangerous for humans. Willett said that ground robots can be harder to figure out how to use than uncrewed aerial vehicles, but "there are equal challenges" with flying drones as well, including the range, battery power, and loitering time. Having enough UAVs to make them expendable is also a challenge. "You need to have enough systems that you could, for example, if you want to observe a particular area, you need to have enough systems in your magazine to be able to put one up and then, before that one runs out of charge, there's another one up to take over the role," he added. With the large amount of drones used by both Ukraine and Russia in mind, Western officials have been considering the need for soldiers to have a large number of drones available to them. One US Army commander said earlier this year that based on his unit's experience, a brigade needed between 1,000 and 1,500 a week in a sustained combat operation. "We need drones at scale. We need to treat them like ammunition," he said at the time. Read the original article on Business Insider

At a recent US-led exercise in the Mojave Desert, thousands of soldiers gathered to try out new technologies, including uncrewed systems. British troops at the training were experimenting with which types of drones were best suited to specific tactics and missions, and shared what they most want from these systems.

Lessons from the exercise included how systems performed in extreme heat and on rugged desert terrain, whether soldiers had enough drones for their missions amid electronic warfare and connectivity issues, and how drones can be most useful.

The British Army's current experimentation unit, the 2nd Battalion, The Yorkshire Regiment, was present at the exercise alongside the unit that will take over their experimentation role, the 1st Battalion Irish Guards. The latter unit also has experience with drones, including a recent exercise with Ukrainian forces. Business Insider also attended the exercises.

Capt. Wick Willett, a mortar platoon commander with the 1st Battalion Irish Guards, said he and his troops had seen the strengths and weaknesses of drones. "I think there are challenges with both air and ground vehicles," Willett told Business Insider, adding that what helps work through those issues are "these robust trials that we're going through now."

The British Army approaches testing of drone systems through two different processes: experimentation and trials. Trials are designed to take a drone, "put it through its paces, and test it to see if it does what the Army wants it to do" before it's acquired, Lt. Col. John Black, commander of the 2nd Battalion of the Yorkshire Regiment, told Business Insider. This includes safety and integration tests.

Experiments are more focused on applying a system to specific use cases, such as ground robots to make front-line logistics easier or safer, or aerial drones for reconnaissance.

In drone experiments, British soldiers see how systems work in specific situations.

US Army photo by Sgt. Nathan Arellano Tlaczani

Willett said he noticed the need for uncrewed ground vehicles to be more consumable, meaning troops could be able to use, lose, or break them more flexibly without worrying about the costs or feasibility of replacing them, "and in order to be consumable, they need to be at a certain price point per unit."

Other soldiers expressed similar sentiments about ground robots, saying the systems could sometimes feel too high-end to use effectively in tactical settings. Black said his experience after testing dozens of UGVs was that the systems were often too expensive to be used in larger volumes and be expended.

Other issues with ground vehicles include driving over certain terrain, the impact of heat on systems and batteries, and the types of missions that are best suited, such as logistics runs and breaches that could be too dangerous for humans.

Willett said that ground robots can be harder to figure out how to use than uncrewed aerial vehicles, but "there are equal challenges" with flying drones as well, including the range, battery power, and loitering time. Having enough UAVs to make them expendable is also a challenge.

"You need to have enough systems that you could, for example, if you want to observe a particular area, you need to have enough systems in your magazine to be able to put one up and then, before that one runs out of charge, there's another one up to take over the role," he added.

With the large amount of drones used by both Ukraine and Russia in mind, Western officials have been considering the need for soldiers to have a large number of drones available to them.

One US Army commander said earlier this year that based on his unit's experience, a brigade needed between 1,000 and 1,500 a week in a sustained combat operation. "We need drones at scale. We need to treat them like ammunition," he said at the time.

items.title: Women in UK arts feel they do not have equal opportunities for roles, says report
items.summary: Exclusive: Research says sector is fixated with young talent, with most women experiencing unconscious bias or sexism Women working in the arts believe they do not have equal opportunities for roles, especially as they get older, according to a report saying that the industry is fixated with “young and emerging” talent. Nearly all (95%) women working in the arts thought gender inequality persisted, while three-quarters (75%) reported experiencing unconscious bias or sexism, according to a survey of 76 arts professionals. More than two-thirds (69%) felt that age negatively affected their career success – a figure that rose to 100% among those working in artistic rather than managerial roles. Continue reading...
